sbh3.2:8.2: Comprehending the meaning, he sees this unattractiveness as established under two divisions: inwardly and outwardly.
sbh3.2:9.1: How does he investigate the specific characteristic?
sbh3.2:9.2: Inwardly, first, he resolves on the unattractiveness within the body as putrid unattractiveness:
sbh3.2:9.3: 'There exist in this body: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, dust, dirt, skin, flesh, bone, sinew, vein, kidneys, heart, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, bowel contents, urine, feces, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fat, lymph, marrow, grease, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, brain, brain-membrane, urine [discharge].'
sbh3.2:9.4: He further resolves that this multifold unattractiveness within the body is comprised by two elements:
sbh3.2:9.5: the earth element and the water element.
sbh3.2:9.7: through feces — this he resolves as the earth element.
sbh3.2:9.8: From [Conjectural: tears and sweat] through urine — this he resolves as the water element.
sbh3.2:10.1: Outwardly, he resolves on the unattractiveness as found outside the body, by way of aspects beginning with the discolored.
sbh3.2:10.3: a corpse he has himself seen,
sbh3.2:10.4: or heard described, or imagined — of a woman, a man, a friend, an enemy, or one indifferent to him;
sbh3.2:10.5: low, middling, or excellent; young, middle-aged, or elderly.
sbh3.2:10.6: Taking the sign, he resolves on a corpse one day dead, the blood drained, [Conjectural: not yet] turned to pus — as the discolored.
sbh3.2:10.7: A corpse two days dead, turned to pus, before worms have arisen — as the festering.
sbh3.2:10.8: A corpse seven days dead, with worms arisen and bloated — as the [Conjectural: bursting] and the swollen.
sbh3.2:10.9: A corpse being eaten by crows, ospreys, vultures, dogs, jackals — as the gnawed.
sbh3.2:10.10: A corpse with skin, flesh, and blood gone, only sinews holding the bones together — as the bloody-skeletal.
sbh3.2:10.11: When the limbs have been scattered in different directions and pulled apart — some with flesh, some without, some with a little flesh left — as the dispersed.

sbh3.2:11.13: The limb-skeleton is the connected arm-bones and thigh-and-leg bones.

sbh3.2:11.21: When he attends to the sign of a real skeleton,
sbh3.2:11.22: then he resolves on the bone-skeleton.

sbh3.2:28.19: rather, on formations arisen from causes, dependently arisen, there is this notion,
sbh3.2:28.20: designation, convention. Thus by dependence-reasoning he investigates.
sbh3.2:28.21: 'Ānāpānasmṛti, frequented and cultivated, conduces to the cutting-off of *vitarka*;
sbh3.2:28.22: this is trustworthy testimony, this is personal [knowing], and this is [Conjectural: the inferential method];
sbh3.2:28.23: this is the established nature-of-things, the unthinkable nature-of-things.' Thus he investigates by cause-and-effect reasoning, by proof-establishing reasoning, and by nature-of-things reasoning.
sbh3.2:29.1: Thus, having investigated the six things with the conduct-purifying object, while again and again calming the inward mind,
sbh3.2:29.2: he again and again investigates that same [object], as it has been investigated, by the modes of vipaśyanā.
sbh3.2:29.3: For him, vipaśyanā purifies on the basis of śamatha.
sbh3.2:29.4: And on the basis of vipaśyanā, śamatha reaches abundance, amplitude.
sbh3.2:29.5: As for the *vipaśyanā* on the skill-object and the defilement-purifying object,
sbh3.2:29.6: I will speak of its working of the six things later, in its own place.
sbh3.2:30.2: and the inverse — ninefold, dark-side-comprised — is also to be known by the yogī.
sbh3.2:30.3: Namely: conformable engagement, practiced engagement, unperverted engagement,
sbh3.2:30.4: non-slack engagement, timely engagement, observation engagement, dissatisfaction engagement, engagement that does not shed the yoke, and right engagement.
sbh3.2:30.5: By this ninefold bright-side-comprised [engagement], the mind is concentrated swiftly, swiftly.
sbh3.2:30.6: And it advances toward excellence in concentration.
sbh3.2:30.7: Whatever stage is to be traversed by it, attained by it — that it reaches quickly, very quickly, without delay.
sbh3.2:30.8: By the dark-side-comprised ninefold engagements, the mind is not concentrated swiftly, swiftly.
sbh3.2:30.9: Nor does it advance toward excellence in concentration.
sbh3.2:30.10: Whatever stage is to be traversed, to be attained — there [the practitioner] delays in going.
sbh3.2:30.12: If [the practitioner] is lust-conducted, he binds the mind to *aśubhā* (unattractiveness);
sbh3.2:30.13: the hatred-conducted [binds it to] *maitrī*; up through the vitarka-conducted [to] *ānāpāna-smṛti*; the balanced-conduct one, lightly-dusted, [binds it to] whatever object has easy uptake (*priyārohatā*) for him.
sbh3.2:30.14: He engages with that [object]. This is conformable engagement.
sbh3.2:30.16: Practice has been done by him, even if only a little, so that he is not in every respect a mere beginner.
sbh3.2:30.17: For one who is a beginner, even when engaged on the conformable object, the hindrances [Conjectural: recur frequently].
sbh3.2:30.18: And [there is] bodily and mental encumbrance,
sbh3.2:30.19: by which his mind is [Conjectural: not] concentrated. This is practiced engagement.
sbh3.2:30.21: He is one engaged continuously, and one engaged respectfully.
sbh3.2:30.22: If he rises from concentration — whether for alms-food, or to attend on a respected teacher,
sbh3.2:30.23: or for the sake of attending a sick person, or for a duty of respect, or any such matter — he does all of it with a mind inclined, tending, leaning toward [the concentration].
sbh3.2:30.24: And having done [the duty] quickly, very quickly, having completed it, he engages again [in meditation],
sbh3.2:30.25: having settled himself for seclusion. If he meets with a gathering of monks, nuns, lay-followers, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas,
sbh3.2:30.26: he does not pass much time in association. He converses moderately.
sbh3.2:30.27: He does not give rise to lengthy speech. He does not withdraw [from his purpose] otherwise.
sbh3.2:30.28: Thus he is one of aroused energy: 'Today indeed I shall attain what is to be attained!'
sbh3.2:30.29: Why so? 'Many are my conditions for death — wind in me might trouble, or bile, or phlegm; food might disagree, by which cholera might settle in my body.
sbh3.2:30.30: Or a snake might bite me; a scorpion or centipede; or fear from a human.' On these occasions, at all times, he [Conjectural: reflects, cultivating the perception of impermanence], and dwells heedful. And thus, further, he dwells heedful:
sbh3.2:30.31: 'Even if I should live seven days, six, five, four, three, two, one day, a watch, a half-watch, an hour, a half-hour —
sbh3.2:30.32: ah, may I live so long as I enjoy alms-food; so long as, having breathed in, I breathe out;
sbh3.2:30.33: and so long as I live, may I undertake yoga in the Teacher's dispensation by yoga and attention.
sbh3.2:30.34: — so that in that much [time] much might be accomplished by me in the Teacher's dispensation.' This is non-slack engagement.
sbh3.2:31.2: From time to time he cultivates the sign of śamatha, [Lacuna] the sign of *pragraha* (lifting up), the sign of *upekṣā* (equanimity).
sbh3.2:31.3: He knows śamatha, the sign of śamatha, and the time of śamatha;
sbh3.2:31.4: [likewise] vipaśyanā, the sign of vipaśyanā, the time of vipaśyanā; pragraha, the sign of pragraha, the time of pragraha;
sbh3.2:31.5: upekṣā, the sign of upekṣā, the time of upekṣā.
sbh3.2:31.6: There, *śamatha* is the ninefold mental abiding.
sbh3.2:31.7: And the mind there is signless, conception-less, calm, very calm, abiding in calm, undivided — hence it is called śamatha.
sbh3.2:31.8: There, the *sign of śamatha* is twofold: the object-sign, and the cause-sign.
sbh3.2:31.9: The image conformable to the knowable thing is the object-sign —
sbh3.2:31.10: by which object he calms that mind. [The cause-sign:] in a mind cultivated by śamatha, for the later purification of śamatha,
sbh3.2:31.11: whatever engagement in vipaśyanā [there is] — this is the cause-sign.
sbh3.2:31.12: What is the *time of śamatha*? Answer: when the mind is excited, or [Conjectural: fears excitement] — that is the time for cultivating śamatha.
sbh3.2:31.13: Likewise when the mind is well-cultivated by vipaśyanā [and is] afflicted by distraction in what is to be done — that is the time for cultivating śamatha.
sbh3.2:31.14: There, *vipaśyanā* has four modes, three doors, and is the investigation of objects subdivided into six things.
sbh3.2:32.1: There, the *sign of vipaśyanā* is twofold: the object-sign and the cause-sign.
sbh3.2:32.2: Among these, the object-sign, the sign of vipaśyanā [Conjectural: on its own side], is the image conformable to the knowable thing — the object-sign,
sbh3.2:32.3: by which object he makes wisdom examine [it].
sbh3.2:32.4: There, the cause-sign: in a mind cultivated by vipaśyanā, for the later purification of vipaśyanā, the [Conjectural: engagement] in calming the mind [is the cause-sign].
sbh3.2:32.5: There, the *time of vipaśyanā*: [Lacuna] when the mind is cultivated by śamatha, and from the very beginning, for understanding the knowable thing as it actually is — that is the time for cultivating vipaśyanā.
sbh3.2:32.7: Whatever — by some pleasing object taken up — is the gladdening, showing-forth, encouraging of the mind.
sbh3.2:32.8: There, the sign-of-pragraha: by which gladdening object as sign the mind is lifted;
sbh3.2:32.9: [and] the arousal of energy conformable to it; there, the time of *pragraha*: when the mind is sunk, or fears sinking — that is the time for cultivating *pragraha*.
sbh3.2:32.11: Whatever mental evenness toward the object, in an undefiled mind, on the śamatha-vipaśyanā side;
sbh3.2:32.13: the workability of a workable mind, the giving-over of the mind, its functioning without exertion.
sbh3.2:32.14: There, the sign-of-upekṣā: that object with which the mind regards [things] with equanimity;
sbh3.2:32.15: and not arousing an excess of energy toward that very object.
sbh3.2:32.16: There, the time of *upekṣā*: when, on the śamatha-vipaśyanā side, the mind is free from sinking and excitement — that is the time for cultivating *upekṣā*.
sbh3.2:33.2: Those very signs are well-grasped, well-discerned, well-taken up —
sbh3.2:33.3: when he wishes, he emerges — the range of concentration,
sbh3.2:33.4: [that is,] the image, he lets go, by attending to the natural object of the [Conjectural: unconcentrated] stage. This is observation engagement.
sbh3.2:33.6: He is not content with wholesome dharmas, and does not [Conjectural: relent]
sbh3.2:33.7: [Conjectural: in striving]; aspiring to a higher, more excellent state, he dwells much [in that].
sbh3.2:33.8: He does not, midway, on account of a small or inferior [attainment], fall into despondency when something higher remains to be done. This is dissatisfaction engagement.
sbh3.2:33.9: What, there, is *engagement that does not shed the yoke*?
sbh3.2:33.10: He does not break the precepts undertaken, does not put holes in them;
sbh3.2:33.11: seeing a young, gracefully-formed, attractive woman, he is not a sign-grasper, not a feature-grasper; he is moderate in food;
sbh3.2:33.12: he is yoked to wakefulness, of few duties, few activities, few preoccupations;
sbh3.2:33.13: he is one who recollects and reminds of what was long-done and long-said.
sbh3.2:33.14: Such kinds of dharmas are called *engagement that does not shed the yoke*.
sbh3.2:33.15: These dharmas are conformable to one-pointedness of mind, [Conjectural: do not shed its yoke], and do not lead to distraction of mind.
sbh3.2:33.16: By them, [the mind is kept] from outward dispersion, from inward mental non-workability. This is engagement that does not shed the yoke.
sbh3.2:34.2: Right engagement is so called because, having resolved and resolved upon the object, he dispels it.
sbh3.2:34.3: If he is engaged in *aśubhā*, he attends to *aśubhā* under aśubhā-modes — by a vipaśyanā that follows only the sign.
sbh3.2:34.4: Then that attention, with that object, should be dispelled again and again, and made present again and again.
sbh3.2:34.5: Now, dispelling is fivefold: by gathering the mind inward; by non-recollection and non-attention; by attention to something else; by attention to the antidote; and by attention to the signless element.
sbh3.2:34.6: There, by the ninefold mental abiding, with vipaśyanā as forerunner, [there is] gathering the mind inward;
sbh3.2:34.7: by [Conjectural: turning away] from all signs from the start, binding [the mind] to non-distraction — [this is] non-recollection and non-attention;
sbh3.2:34.8: [passing] from the concentrated-stage object to another concentrated-stage object, while attending [only to] the concentrated stage — [this is] attention to something else;
sbh3.2:34.9: [attending to] *aśubhā* as antidote to beauty, up through *ānāpānasmṛti* as antidote to *vitarka*;
sbh3.2:34.10: [attending to] the space-element as antidote to form — [this is] attention to the antidote.
sbh3.2:34.11: From the non-attention to all signs and from the attention to the signless element — [this is] attention to the signless element.
sbh3.2:34.12: Moreover, though the character of dispelling has been laid out comprehensively for that object, what is intended in the present context is [dispelling] by gathering [the sign] inward and by non-recollection and non-attention.
sbh3.2:34.13: There, by a beginner, by one in his first attempt at engagement, the mind should not, from the start, be bound to any object — neither *aśubhā* nor another — except only [to this, so as not to be distracted]:
sbh3.2:34.14: 'Is my mind signless, conception-less, calm, very calm, unagitated, unwavering, not eager, free of effort, inwardly delighted?'
sbh3.2:34.15: Thus engaged, with respect to all external signs as they arise and arise, he practises non-recollection and non-attention. This is his dispelling of the object by non-recollection and non-attention.
sbh3.2:35.1: Practising yoga there, he takes in [delight]; and again he ranges over the [Conjectural: sign-bearing], conceptual object — *aśubhā* and the rest.
sbh3.2:35.2: And how does he range? By a vipaśyanā that follows the sign alone, that follows seeking and reviewing.
sbh3.2:35.3: And he is not exclusively engaged in vipaśyanā.
sbh3.2:35.4: Turning back again from the sign of vipaśyanā, he attends to that same object in the mode of śamatha.
sbh3.2:35.5: then that object is for him [Conjectural: neither] released nor taken up —
sbh3.2:35.6: because that object is what śamatha proceeds on, hence not released;
sbh3.2:35.7: because he does not make it a sign, does not conceptualize it, hence not taken up. Thus by gathering [the mind] inward he dispels the object.
sbh3.2:35.8: There, for one who has taken up the sign of vipaśyanā again — the object [that is] the sign of the knowable thing — if he only resolves upon the object
sbh3.2:35.9: and does not dispel it again and again, his resolve does not, in succession, become purer, clearer,
sbh3.2:35.10: [it does not] proceed toward direct apprehension of the knowable thing.
sbh3.2:35.11: But when he resolves again and again and dispels again and again, his resolve becomes purer and purest in succession, proceeding to direct apprehension of the knowable thing.
sbh3.2:35.12: Just as a painter, or a painter's apprentice, first engaged in the painter's craft,
sbh3.2:35.13: having received from the teacher a model-image preceded by instruction, makes a copy after looking at it again and again;
sbh3.2:35.14: having made it, again and again he erases it, destroys it, and makes it afresh;
sbh3.2:35.15: the more he breaks [it] up and remakes [it], the purer, the clearer his next picture appears.
sbh3.2:35.16: Thus indeed, by right-engagement, in time he attains equality with the teacher, or even surpasses him.
sbh3.2:35.17: If, on the other hand, he were to make that picture again and again on top of [the previous one] without erasing, he would [Conjectural: never] attain purity of that picture. The same principle is to be known here.
sbh3.2:35.18: There, whatever object he resolves upon, that he dispels; but not necessarily, whatever he dispels, does he resolve upon.
sbh3.2:35.19: He resolves on the limited and dispels only the limited; so too [for] the extended and the [Conjectural: measureless].
sbh3.2:35.20: Having dispelled the limited, he sometimes resolves only on the limited, sometimes only on the extended, [sometimes] only on the [Conjectural: measureless]; and the same is to be understood for the extended and the [Conjectural: measureless].
sbh3.2:35.21: There, of form-dharmas, whatever is sign, image, appearance — that is gross, like a magical creation; or, of formless dharmas, the appearance that is preceded by name-convention and governed by what has been experienced. This is called
sbh3.2:35.23: This is the ninefold bright-side engagement, conformable to śamatha-vipaśyanā — to be known [thus].
sbh3.2:35.24: Likewise, in turn, [there is] just the ninefold inverse-mode [dark-side].
sbh3.2:35.25: Thus by the dark-and-bright-side classification, [there is] the eighteenfold engagement. This is called *one-pointedness*.
sbh3.2:36.2: Answer: by four causes, the yogī thus right-engaged purifies his own mind of obstacles.
sbh3.2:36.3: By full-knowledge of own-nature; by [knowledge] of the cause; by full-knowledge of the danger; and by cultivation of the antidote.
sbh3.2:36.4: What, then, is the own-nature of obstacle?
sbh3.2:36.5: Answer: there are four obstacles — *paritamanā* (despondency), *nivaraṇa* (hindrance), *vitarka* (discursive thought), and *ātmasaṁpragraha* (self-exaltation).
sbh3.2:36.6: There, *paritamanā* is the defiled longing, dissatisfaction — yearning, dejection, distress — of one engaged in renunciation and seclusion.
sbh3.2:36.7: There, *nivaraṇa* is the five hindrances beginning with sense-desire.
sbh3.2:36.8: There, *vitarka* is sense-desire-vitarka and the like — defiled vitarkas.
sbh3.2:36.9: There, *ātmasaṁpragraha* is when, by a trifling, an inferior, a mere touch of knowledge-and-vision, he exalts himself: 'I am a gainer; others are not so.'
sbh3.2:36.10: As before, in detail, this is the own-nature of obstacle.
sbh3.2:37.1: There, of *paritamanā* there are six causes:
sbh3.2:37.2: namely, weakness of the basis, through the dominance of previous karma or through the affliction of disease; excessive engagement; deficient engagement; initial engagement; abundance of defilements; and non-practice of seclusion.
sbh3.2:37.3: For *nivaraṇa*, *vitarka*, and *ātmasaṁpragraha*: with respect to the dharmas that are the locus of hindrance, of [Conjectural: vitarka], of self-exaltation, unwise attention, much practised, is the cause of hindrance, vitarka, and self-exaltation.
sbh3.2:37.4: Not attending to unattractiveness, [the practitioner] attends to attractiveness — this here is unwise.
sbh3.2:37.5: Likewise, [Conjectural: not] attending to *maitrī*, [Lacuna]; abandoning the perception of light with its sign, he attends to the sign of darkness; not attending to śamatha, [he attends to] thoughts of relatives, of the country, of not dying, and of former play, laughter, delight, dalliance.
sbh3.2:37.6: Not attending to *idaṁ-pratyayatā pratītyasamutpāda*, he attends, with respect to what belongs to the three times, to an improper perception, 'I' or 'mine': this here is unwise [attention].
sbh3.2:37.8: When this fourfold obstacle is present, what has not been attained is not attained; from what has been attained, [he] falls back;
sbh3.2:37.9: he falls from yoga-engagement; he becomes defiled-dwelling, pain-dwelling; he reproaches himself; and is reproached by others;
sbh3.2:37.10: and at the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the unfortunate states. This is the danger here.
sbh3.2:37.12: The antidote to *paritamanā*, in brief, is the *recollections*.
sbh3.2:37.13: By attention to recollection, having gladdened the mind, having gladdened [it], he dispels arisen *paritamanā* and does not produce [it] unarisen.
sbh3.2:37.14: There, for bodily weakness, [Conjectural: excessive engagement], and initial engagement, the antidote is evenness of energy.
sbh3.2:37.15: For deficient engagement, the antidote is willingness to listen and careful inquiry.
sbh3.2:37.16: [For] abundance of defilements — the antidote is engagement of the *aśubhā* and other objects as appropriate.
sbh3.2:37.17: [For] non-practice — the antidote is just such a [reflective] consideration:
sbh3.2:37.18: 'I have not previously practiced seclusion-cultivation, by which now in me, engaged in seclusion, *paritamanā* arises.
sbh3.2:37.19: If I do not undertake the practice now, then in future it will again be of just this kind.
sbh3.2:37.20: Having considered, dissatisfaction must be abandoned by me; delight must be made.' For the [Conjectural: remaining], hindrance and the rest, the cultivation of wise attention, the reverse of unwise attention, is to be known as the antidote.
sbh3.2:37.21: There, having fully known the own-nature — as obstruction, as defilement, as belonging to the dark side: 'this is to be avoided' —
sbh3.2:37.22: And [recognizing] 'its avoidance is by avoidance of [its] cause,' he investigates the cause.
sbh3.2:37.23: And '[on the other hand,] of what is to be avoided, what is the fault if it is not avoided?' — thence he investigates the danger.
sbh3.2:37.24: 'How is non-arising in the future, of what has been avoided?' — thence he cultivates the antidote. Thus the mind is purified by him from obstacles.
sbh3.2:38.1: There, as far as there is abundance of teaching conformable to vipaśyanā, so far there is abundance of vipaśyanā; and as far as there is abundance of vipaśyanā, so far there is abundance of śamatha. And this vipaśyanā is to be known as endless, [Conjectural: through the endlessness of the knowable] —
sbh3.2:38.2: namely, through these three gateways, in the one-by-one [investigation] of the six things, by the method of entry into endless modes —
sbh3.2:38.3: and so as vipaśyanā, when one is rightly engaged, reaches extension, growth, amplitude — taking the power of purity of practice as governing — so likewise the śamatha-side, productive of body-and-mind pliancy, is to be known to reach extension, growth, amplitude.
sbh3.2:38.4: As his body becomes pliant, and his mind, so too the basis of one-pointedness of mind on the object increases;
sbh3.2:38.5: as one-pointedness of mind increases, so the body becomes pliant, and the mind;
sbh3.2:38.6: thus these two dharmas are arisen from one another, bound to one another — namely, one-pointedness of mind [and pliancy of body and mind]; [from them comes] the arising of direct knowledge.
sbh3.2:38.7: There, to what extent is *aśubhā* attained? To what extent up through *ānāpānasmṛti*? — and so on.
sbh3.2:38.8: As to this: for this yogī, as a consequence of frequenting, cultivating, and making much of the engagement with *aśubhā* — whether walking or abiding, even with the object before [him], even while examining signs, by nature and without effort — unattractiveness appears more abundantly.
sbh3.2:38.9: And, by reason of the well-cultivation of *aśubhā*, the mind does not leap toward, does not become pleased with, does not resolve upon, dharmas connected with sense-lust — equanimity stands by; disgust and repugnance [are] to be known.
sbh3.2:38.10: By the yogī [it is to be known]: '*Aśubhā* has been reached by me; the fruit of cultivation has been attained by me.' To this extent *aśubhā* is attained; by the opposite it is to be known as unattained.
sbh3.2:38.11: As with *aśubhā*, so likewise *maitrī*, *idaṁ-pratyayatā pratītyasamutpāda*, *dhātuprabheda*, and *ānāpānasmṛti* are to be known.
sbh3.2:38.12: Here is the distinction: loving-mindedness appears more abundantly, not the sign of aversion; the mind does not leap toward dharmas connected with ill-will — and so on in detail.
sbh3.2:38.13: Impermanence, painfulness, and non-self appear more abundantly, not the sign of delusion accompanied by the view of permanence, pleasure, and a self; the mind does not leap toward dharmas connected with delusion — and so on in detail.
sbh3.2:38.14: The perception of the diversity of elements, of [Conjectural: there being no single element], of the distinctions of the body appears more abundantly, not the perception of the [Conjectural: body as one mass]; the mind does not leap toward dharmas connected with conceit — and so on in detail.
sbh3.2:38.15: The perception of inward calm, the perception of śamatha, appears more abundantly, not the perception of proliferation; the mind does not leap toward dharmas connected with vitarka — and so on in detail.
sbh3.2:39.1: There, [Conjectural: to what extent] do śamatha and vipaśyanā, both [Conjectural: blended], proceed in equal yoke,
sbh3.2:39.2: so that the path is called 'going yoked' (*yuganaddhavāhin*)?
sbh3.2:39.3: Answer: one who is a gainer of the ninth mode of the ninefold mental abiding — namely, of the concentrated state —
sbh3.2:39.4: having relied on that consummated samādhi, engages, by higher wisdom, in vipaśyanā of dharmas.
sbh3.2:39.5: For him, seeing into dharmas at that time, the path proceeds of its own accord, without exertion;
sbh3.2:39.6: without effort, vipaśyanā, purified and cleansed, proceeds made pliant and embraced in conformity with śamatha.
sbh3.2:39.7: [Conjectural: To this extent] it is said that his śamatha and vipaśyanā, both [Conjectural: blended], proceed in equal yoke,
sbh3.2:39.8: and the path becomes one going yoked with śamatha and vipaśyanā.
sbh3.2:40.2: Sign-grasping, seeking, and reviewing follow as the gateways;
sbh3.2:40.3: by meaning, by characteristics, by [Conjectural: things], by sides, and by times together with reasonings;
sbh3.2:40.5: timely, observation, [Conjectural: dissatisfaction], not shedding the yoke — [these are] the engagements;
sbh3.2:40.6: and right engagement: these nine grounds are held to be of two kinds;
sbh3.2:40.7: from own-nature, from cause, likewise from seeing the danger,
sbh3.2:40.8: and from the cultivation of the antidote — the purification of obstacles.
sbh3.2:41.2: Answer: the beginner, the one engaged for the first time in this work, having had the pervasive characteristic established for him with respect to one-pointedness and the purification from obstacles, avoids wrong engagement and trains in right engagement.
sbh3.2:41.3: From the very first, [thinking] 'I shall attain one-pointedness and delight-in-abandonment,' he engages by four kinds of attention.
sbh3.2:41.4: By which four? By the *citta-saṁtāpana* (mind-heating) attention, the *citta-abhiṣyandana* (mind-suffusing) attention, the *praśrabdhi-janaka* (pliancy-producing) attention, and the *jñāna-darśana-viśodhana* (knowledge-and-vision-purifying) attention.
sbh3.2:41.6: Answer: that attention by which he stirs up the mind with respect to stirring-up-worthy dharmas — this is the mind-heating attention.
sbh3.2:41.8: That pleasing attention by which he gladdens the mind — this is the mind-suffusing attention.
sbh3.2:41.10: Answer: that attention by which, from time to time having stirred up the mind with respect to stirring-up-worthy dharmas, and from time to time having gladdened the mind with respect to gladdening-worthy dharmas, he then inwardly calms [the mind];
sbh3.2:41.11: in the signless, conception-less, he establishes [the mind] thus, makes one-pointed mindfulness proceed;
sbh3.2:41.12: by which cause, by which condition — as antidote to body-and-mind encumbrance, producing gladness in body-and-mind — body-pliancy and mind-pliancy arise.
sbh3.2:41.13: This is called the pliancy-producing attention.
sbh3.2:41.15: That attention by which, from time to time, with the mind thus [Conjectural: inwardly calmed], he again and again applies himself, by higher wisdom, to vipaśyanā of dharmas —
sbh3.2:41.16: namely, having relied on that very inward *cetaḥ-śamatha* — this is called the knowledge-and-vision-purifying attention.
sbh3.2:42.1: He, from time to time, stirs up the mind with respect to stirring-up-worthy dharmas; thus his mind becomes heated, well-heated, agitated, well-agitated — namely, with respect to the dharmas that are the locus of the outflows.
sbh3.2:42.2: What are all the stirring-up-worthy places?
sbh3.2:42.3: Answer: four. Namely, *ātma-vipatti* (one's own misfortune) and *para-vipatti* (the misfortune of others) — in the present, when at hand, when face-to-face, [taken up] in consequence of wise attention, [each] becomes a stirring-up-worthy place.
sbh3.2:42.4: And there [the contrary pair]: one's own success and others' success — in the past, when ceased, gone, transformed, [taken up] in consequence of wise attention, [each] becomes a stirring-up-worthy place.
sbh3.2:42.5: From time to time he gladdens the mind with respect to gladdening-worthy dharmas. When he gladdens [the mind], his mind thus becomes oily, moist, fluid, clear, serene.
sbh3.2:42.7: Answer: three bases of gladdening: the Jewels (*ratnāni*), purity of the trainings (*śikṣāpada-pāriśuddhi*), and the non-shrinking of a mind born of confident expectation of distinctive attainment in oneself.
sbh3.2:42.8: Recollecting the Jewels, he gladdens the mind thus: 'Gains are well-gained by me — I whose Teacher is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One;
sbh3.2:42.9: gains are well-gained — that I have gone forth in the well-stated dharma-vinaya;
sbh3.2:42.10: gains are well-gained — whose fellow brahmacāris are virtuous, possessed of qualities, lovely, of beautiful dharmas.
sbh3.2:42.11: My death will be auspicious, my time-of-passing auspicious, my future auspicious.'
sbh3.2:42.12: Thus, recollecting these four, he gladdens the mind.
sbh3.2:43.1: How does he gladden the mind while recollecting *purity of the trainings*, *purity of virtue*?
sbh3.2:43.2: 'Gains are well-gained by me — I, in respect of the Teacher the Tathāgata Arhat Fully Awakened One, and his well-stated dharma-vinaya, and the well-practicing disciples' saṁgha therein — I am with these fellow brahmacāris of common virtue, of common training, with loving body, speech, and mental action, of common view, of common enjoyment.'
sbh3.2:43.3: Thus recollecting purity of the trainings, purity of virtue, he gladdens the mind — namely, by joy preceded by [Conjectural: non-regret].
sbh3.2:43.4: How, by relying on the confident expectation of one's own attainment: 'I am capable, of such pure virtue;
sbh3.2:43.5: I am able and a fit vessel. With these fellow brahmacāris of common virtue, common view, and with these good [people] of common course, gone rightly, true persons, I am capable of being thus, of so engaging, of attaining the unattained, realizing the unrealized, directly experiencing the not-yet-directly-experienced in this very life.' Thus he generates joy — by relying on the basis of confident expectation of one's own attainment, he gladdens the mind.
sbh3.2:44.1: Moreover: by whatever distinctive attainment has been made by him while abiding with energy begun afresh after a previous [phase],
sbh3.2:44.2: recollecting that and confidently apprehending further distinctive attainment, he gladdens the mind — this is the further basis.
sbh3.2:44.3: Heating the mind with respect to stirring-up-worthy dharmas, he turns the mind away from outflow-stationed dharmas, makes it inverse [to them], establishes it facing-away, separates it.
sbh3.2:44.4: Gladdening, suffusing the mind with respect to gladdening-worthy dharmas, he turns the mind, with affection, toward dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion; he attaches [the mind] to them, delights [the mind] in them, conjoins [the mind] with them.
sbh3.2:44.5: Thus, by these two dharmas, his mind proceeds — turned away from all dark-side, turned toward all bright-side — namely, by *saṁvega* (urgency) and *praharṣa* (gladness).
sbh3.2:44.6: Since the mind, thus turned away from the dark side by the mind-heating attention and turned toward the bright side by the mind-suffusing attention, from time to time is inwardly applied — namely, by *cetaḥ-śamatha* with the pliancy-producing attention —
sbh3.2:44.7: from time to time he discerns dharmas, examines, ponders, investigates — by the knowledge-and-vision-purifying attention.
sbh3.2:44.8: Thus his mind, from time to time embraced by śamatha and vipaśyanā, made fit as the cause of all aspects and all qualities, after the passing of those nights and days, of instants, *lavas*, and *muhūrtas*, advances toward distinction.
sbh3.2:45.1: Just as raw gold or silver, by a skilled smith or by a smith's apprentice, when from time to time it has been heated, so that stain and dross are gone, and quenched, is made fit for this or that work of ornament by being soft and workable —
sbh3.2:45.2: the skilled smith or the smith's apprentice, with the craft-knowledge suited to it and the tools of his craft, works it into whatever ornamental form is desired —
sbh3.2:45.3: just so, when the yogī's mind has been agitated by being turned away from the stains and dross of covetousness and the rest, and gladdened by being turned away from defiled-dejection,
sbh3.2:45.4: then wherever the yogī directs it — to the śamatha-side or the vipaśyanā-side — there [the mind] becomes well-attached, well-clinging, undivided, unshaking;
sbh3.2:45.5: and it advances toward the perfecting of the intended purpose.
sbh3.2:46.1: There, how is the beginner, the one in his first attempt at this work, instructed in *manaskāra-bhāvanā*?
sbh3.2:46.2: [The way is] that he, being instructed and engaging, first touches delight in abandonment (*prahāṇābhirati*) and one-pointedness of mind.
sbh3.2:46.3: Here the knower of yoga (*yogajña*) at the very first instructs the beginner engaged in yoga thus:
sbh3.2:46.4: 'Come, dear one — relying on the three causes that take up signs, namely what is seen, what is heard, or a conception governed by thought and inference, take up five signs:
sbh3.2:46.5: the urgency-generating (*saṁvejanīya*), the gladdening (*prasadanīya*), the danger sign, the luminous sign, and the sign of discerning the thing (*vasturūpaṇā*).
sbh3.2:46.6: If that beginner engaged in yoga is of lust-conduct, suited to be led by *aśubhā* — how is he to be awakened to the taking up of the five signs?
sbh3.2:46.7: He is to be awakened thus: 'Come, dear one. Whatever village or town you dwell in dependent on: if you hear of someone, man or woman, in another village or town who is afflicted — pained, gravely ill, or dead — man or woman;
sbh3.2:46.8: or any friend, minister, relative, or kinsman of that man or woman; or the loss of [Conjectural: wealth] of the people of that village, caused by an enemy army, by burning by fire, by being carried off by water, by ruin through bad management, by the collapse of ill-run business, by the arrival of an unwelcome heir, or by ruin through a wastrel of the family;
sbh3.2:46.9: or if you do not hear [of it] but see [it] directly.
sbh3.2:46.10: or not in another village or town but in this very one; or not in this village or town and not of others, but you yourself are touched by bodily feelings, painful and sharp' — and so on in detail as before.
sbh3.2:46.11: 'Having seen, heard all this, stir up the mind: ‘Painful indeed is this saṁsāra, hard-won this individual-existence-attainment, in which such forms of misfortune — one's own and others' — are met with.
sbh3.2:46.12: Namely: misfortune of health, of [Conjectural: relatives], of wealth; sickness and the nature of sickness; death and the nature of death. Furthermore, for some, misfortune of virtue and of view, by reason of which beings here and now become pain-dwellers, and in the future are bound for unfortunate destinies.
sbh3.2:46.13: And whatever fortunes [there are] for here-and-now happy-dwelling and for fortunate destinies in the future — these too are impermanent; their impermanence is to be discerned.
sbh3.2:46.14: If misfortune is face-to-face, fortune at that time is turned-away. Even when misfortune is not face-to-face, fortune is hard to obtain and of perishable nature.’'
sbh3.2:46.15: And thus, having agitated the mind, wisely and well, you should apply [yourself] wisely:
sbh3.2:46.16: 'This situation cannot be relied on, cannot be trusted: that for me, wandering in saṁsāra, not finally released, my mind not liberated, these misfortunes and fortunes would not come before me, or would turn away from me;
sbh3.2:46.17: nor that suffering — sharp, harsh, bitter, unspeakable — would not arise for me from this cause: there is no such case. Therefore, taking all this as governing, I must be one delighting in abandonment, heedful.
sbh3.2:46.18: And dwelling much thus, I shall make [Conjectural: an end] of this harm.' Thus apply yourself wisely. Thus, having taken up the urgency-generating sign, take up next the gladdening sign.
sbh3.2:47.1: And again, take it up thus — examine your own virtues:
sbh3.2:47.2: 'Are my precepts pure, or impure? Is there any transgression of training — through forgetfulness, lack of respect, abundance of defilement, or by being uninstructed?
sbh3.2:47.3: Or, having transgressed, have I made amends as the dharma directs, and with [right] intention generated the mental resolve not to do [it] again?
sbh3.2:47.4: Have I done what should be done; have I left undone what should not be done, in brief? Am I one of accomplished intention and accomplished engagement — namely, in the trainings?'
sbh3.2:47.5: Thus, as you examine, if the aggregate of virtue is pure, you need not form the volition 'May [Conjectural: non-regret] arise in me'; rather, it is simply the nature of things that for one of pure virtue non-regret arises.
sbh3.2:47.6: Likewise, for one without regret, the volition should not be made: 'May joy arise in me!' For by the nature of things, joy arises for the non-regretting one.
sbh3.2:47.7: By this one basis of gladdening, joy preceded by [Conjectural: pure] non-regret is to be generated.
sbh3.2:47.8: Having generated [joy], by another base of further gladdening — gladden the mind.
sbh3.2:47.9: If, then, you have, after a previous [attainment], become [one with] even a limited further distinctive attainment, joy is to be generated: 'I am capable, able. Thus, of pure virtue, well-established in the trainings of the Blessed One —
sbh3.2:47.10: in this very life, for the attainment of what is [Conjectural: not yet] attained, the attainment of the unrealized, the realization of the not-yet-realized.' By this basis too, gladden the mind.
sbh3.2:47.11: And if you have, after a previous [attainment], become a gainer of even a [Conjectural: small] distinctive attainment, then, taking that as governing, with confidence in the complete distinctive attainment of others — namely the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata's disciples — and in your own further distinctive attainment, gladden the mind.
sbh3.2:47.12: Whatever mental [delight] arises from these modes — this is *praharṣa* (gladness).
sbh3.2:47.13: Whatever [delight arises] from these modes — this is called *prīti-manaskatā* (mind-delightedness) of the previously-gladdened one.
sbh3.2:48.1: Thus he has him take up the gladdening sign, and having done so, instructs him further:
sbh3.2:48.2: 'Come, dear one. With mind heated by the urgency-generating sign, with mind suffused by the gladdening-sign — having abandoned covetousness and dejection in the world, you shall abide abundantly.
sbh3.2:48.3: Wherever you engage in the object — on the śamatha-side or the vipaśyanā-side — there, on that object, the mind shall stand.
sbh3.2:48.4: Inwardly well-established, you shall attain body-pliancy, mind-pliancy, mind-one-pointedness.'
sbh3.2:48.5: Thus, for one turned away from the dark side and turned toward the bright side — namely, through urgency and suffusion — take up next, in full, the danger sign (*ādīnava-nimitta*): namely from the signs, from the [Conjectural: vitarkas], and from the defilements.
sbh3.2:48.6: There: signs are the ten beginning with form-sign; vitarkas are the eight beginning with sense-desire-vitarka; defilements are the five beginning with sense-desire.
sbh3.2:48.7: And of these, take up the danger thus: 'These signs are makers of activity for the mind. These vitarkas are makers of agitation, loosing the mind. These defilements are makers of non-calm for the mind.
sbh3.2:48.8: Whatever activity of the mind is made by signs, whatever loosing-agitation is made by vitarka, whatever non-calm is made by defilement — this is the painful dwelling of the mind.
sbh3.2:48.9: Therefore these signs, vitarkas, defilements are painful, ignoble, harm-bringing, mind-scattering and agitating.'
sbh3.2:48.10: Thus having taken up the danger sign, in one-pointedness of mind, in mental abiding, in non-distraction of mind, take up the sign through six modes: by the perception of the [Conjectural: signless]; in the signless, by the perception of non-activity; by the perception of the non-conceptual; in the non-conceptual, by the perception of no longing and no agitation; by the perception of calm; in calm, by the perception of the [Conjectural: pleasure] of extinction free of burning.
sbh3.2:49.1: Thus having taken up the sign, take up next the luminous sign (*āloka-nimitta*): from a lamp, from the brightness of a mass of fire, from the sun's disc, or from the moon's disc. Having taken up the sign, go to a charnel-ground and take up the sign from a livid corpse,
sbh3.2:49.2: up through bones or a skeleton; or, failing the charnel-ground, take up the sign from one made as a painting or [Conjectural: of wood or stone].
sbh3.2:49.3: Having taken up [the sign], approach the sitting-place — go to a forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty hut; sit on a couch, a seat, or a grass-mat.
sbh3.2:49.4: Cross your legs, wash your feet, hold the body straight, establish mindfulness to the fore, and sit. From the very first, make [the mind] bound by mindfulness, in one-pointedness, in non-distraction of mind.
sbh3.2:49.5: There, [develop] the six perceptions — [Lacuna] the perception of the non-conceptual, the perception of calm, the perception of non-activity, the perception of no longing and no agitation, and the perception of the [Conjectural: pleasure] of extinction free of burning.
sbh3.2:49.6: And there, let the awareness-of-distraction-and-non-distraction be present — by which awareness, in whichever signs, vitarkas, defilements [arise], you know distraction; and in mental one-pointedness, accompanied by the cultivation of the six perceptions, [know] non-distraction.
sbh3.2:49.7: And there, attentive to distraction-and-non-distraction, be such that your continuum and mental flow — bound to one-pointedness, bound inwardly to *cetaḥ-śamatha* — proceeds successively, signless, conception-less, calm.
sbh3.2:49.8: If, through forgetfulness, when the mind has thus reached śamatha, signs, vitarkas, and defilements, through the fault of non-practice, come into appearance, [Conjectural: like a face in a mirror], and make themselves [your] object —
sbh3.2:49.9: non-attention through non-recollection should be made toward them whenever they arise — namely, taking what was seen before [the danger] as governing, that object will be dispelled by non-attention through non-recollection and securely settled in non-appearance.
sbh3.2:49.10: Dear one, this is the subtle object — hard for [you] to penetrate. For your penetration, sharp desire and exertion are to be made.
sbh3.2:50.1: It was with reference to this object that the Blessed One said:
sbh3.2:50.2: 'Bhikkhus, [crying] ‘Country-beauty! Country-beauty!’ — a great crowd of people would assemble.
sbh3.2:50.3: Then a man would come, not of foolish kind. To him someone would say:
sbh3.2:50.4: ‘Sir, this oil-vessel, full to the brim, not to be spilled, is to be carried by you between the assembled crowd — between that country-beauty and the great gathering.
sbh3.2:50.5: And an executioner with raised sword follows close behind you. If you let fall even a single drop from this oil-vessel onto the ground, the executioner with raised sword will cut off your head at the root!’
sbh3.2:50.6: What do you think, bhikkhus — would that man, not attending to the oil-vessel, not attending to the executioner with raised sword, attend to the country-beauty or the great gathering?'
sbh3.2:50.7: 'No, no, Bhadanta! Why so? Because that man has seen the executioner with raised sword following close behind him.
sbh3.2:50.8: He would think: ‘If I let fall even a single drop from this oil-vessel onto the ground, this executioner with raised sword will cut off my head at the root!’
sbh3.2:50.9: Rather, that man — not attending to the country-beauty or the great gathering — would carry just that oil-vessel with his whole mind brought to bear, and would carry it rightly.'
sbh3.2:50.10: 'Just so, bhikkhus — those who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness carefully, with esteem, with the whole mind brought to bear — these are my disciples.'
sbh3.2:50.11: There, '*country-beauty*' is the name for the dharmas that are occasions for obsession by the secondary defilements beginning with sensual desire.
sbh3.2:50.12: '*The supreme dance, song, and music*' is the name for the dharmas that are occasions for agitation by thought and proliferation.
sbh3.2:50.13: '*The great gathering*' is the name for the ten signs beginning with the form-sign.
sbh3.2:50.14: '*The man not of foolish kind*' is the name for the *yogācāra*.
sbh3.2:50.15: '*The oil-vessel*' is the name for the mind bound to śamatha — in the sense of its being made supple by pliancy of body and mind.
sbh3.2:50.16: '*The executioner with raised sword*' is the name for the danger previously taken up with respect to signs, vitarkas, and secondary defilements.
sbh3.2:50.17: 'He attends carefully and does not let even one drop fall to the ground' — this is the name for the śamatha-path held by attentiveness with full knowledge of distraction and non-distraction, by which he makes the whole mind-continuum, the mind-stream, proceed signless, non-conceptual, calm, by the power of energy, without a break, in unbroken continuity.
sbh3.2:50.18: And he does not produce even one mind that has a sign as its object, or a vitarka or a secondary defilement as its object.
sbh3.2:51.1: The yogī instructs the beginner thus engaged in śamatha:
sbh3.2:51.2: 'So long, dear one, as your mind, thus engaged in the śamatha-path, is held by [proper] means, accompanied by mindfulness and clear comprehension, and delighted — so long should you cultivate the śamatha-path itself.
sbh3.2:51.3: If, through the fault of lack of practice, [the mind] does not delight and that object [comes to presence only] with contrivance, then, emerging from the non-conceptual object, he binds mindfulness to a conceptual object.
sbh3.2:51.4: That very *aśubhā*-sign you previously took up — attend to that very one, from the start, by a vipaśyanā that follows the sign alone: namely the discolored, or the festering, up to the skeleton.
sbh3.2:51.5: And thus engaged, from the very first resolve on one discolored [corpse], up to one skeleton.
sbh3.2:51.6: When you have made yourself familiar with this, and your resolve proceeds luminous — [resolve] on that object as two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred discolored [corpses], a thousand discolored [corpses], up to all directions and intermediate directions, in the [Conjectural: measureless] mode, resolve [on them] as [Conjectural: full] and uninterrupted,
sbh3.2:51.7: where there is no gap [left], not even the size of the tip of a staff.
sbh3.2:51.8: As with the discolored [corpses], so up to the skeletons — all in this way. Relying on resolve-attention, enter real attention.
sbh3.2:51.9: And enter again thus: ‘As many as these discolored [corpses] are, up to skeletons, that I have resolved on — measurelessly more are, for me, beginning from the prior limit, in this and that existence, destiny, death, and rebirth, the discolored [corpses] that have come to be of me, dead and deceased, up to the skeletons that have come to be —
sbh3.2:51.10: whose prior limit is not discerned as I transmigrate; if anyone were to gather them, and gathered they did not perish or putrefy, there is no region of earth where they would have room.
sbh3.2:51.11: [Even] those of a single kalpa, up to skeletons — if anyone were to gather them, the heap of them gathered would equal Mount Vipulapārśva.
sbh3.2:51.12: As from the prior limit, so too from the later limit — for as long as I do not make an end of suffering.’ Thus indeed you should apply yourself.
sbh3.2:51.13: Relying on [Conjectural: resolve-]attention, you will enter real attention.'
sbh3.2:51.14: And these discolored [corpses], up to skeletons, are not to be viewed all at once by one engaged in vipaśyanā. Rather, having resolved on one discolored [corpse], he should again calm the mind; and he should resolve on that discolored [corpse] only so long as [the mind] on that object is delighted and luminous and is not beset by strain.
sbh3.2:51.15: [Conjectural: When it comes to presence only with strain,] at that time [the mind] should be calmed inwardly. As with the discolored [corpse], so up to one skeleton; and so up to the measureless, by this very method, it is to be understood.
sbh3.2:51.16: Having calmed the mind inwardly, [Conjectural: calm is to be resolved upon]; then, last of all, the measureless discolored [corpses], the measureless [others] up to skeletons, he dispels by gathering the mind inward, and settles them in non-appearance.
sbh3.2:51.17: And he does not let go of those conceptual signs, nor does he conceptualize [them]; rather, he settles the mind on that very object, signless, non-conceptual, calm.
sbh3.2:52.2: 'Dear one, that luminous sign you previously took up — attend to that too, in the engagement on the śamatha side and in the engagement on the vipaśyanā side. With a mind accompanied by light, accompanied by brightness, luminous, free of darkness, cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā.
sbh3.2:52.3: And as you thus cultivate the perception of light on the path of śamatha and vipaśyanā: if from the very start your resolve on the object is unclear, [Conjectural: faint in appearance], then by that cause, that condition, [Conjectural: the resolve from cultivation too will be unclear, and faint in appearance];
sbh3.2:52.4: but if from the very start it is clear and abundant in appearance, it will go on to become, in greater measure, clearer and more abundant in appearance.'
sbh3.2:52.5: With the urgency sign well taken up, the gladdening sign, the śamatha sign, the vipaśyanā sign, and the luminous sign well taken up — from time to time calming the mind inwardly, from time to time investigating dharmas by a vipaśyanā that follows the sign alone — enter the foundations of mindfulness:
sbh3.2:52.6: namely, taking the *aśubhā*-practice as governing, and thus investigating, having taken up outwardly, from the body, the sign of the thirty-six substances, from hair down to urine, resolve on all these inwardly too as impure substances, and inwardly calm the mind —
sbh3.2:52.7: this will be for you the essence of the inward contemplation of the body in the body, namely beginning from your own inner body.
sbh3.2:52.8: And again outwardly — having taken up the *aśubhā*-sign, resolve on a discolored [corpse], up to bones or a skeleton, by limited, extended, or measureless resolve; resolving again and again, inwardly calm the mind.
sbh3.2:52.9: This will be for you the essence of the outward contemplation of the body in the body, namely beginning from the outer body belonging to another's continuum.
sbh3.2:52.10: And again, with a mind imbued with unattractiveness in your own inner body, and with a mind imbued with unattractiveness, inner and outer, in another's body, resolve on yourself as dying, or dead and being carried out to the charnel-ground, or carried out and cast away at the charnel-ground, or cast away and in the discolored state, the festering state, up to the skeleton state.
sbh3.2:52.11: This will be for you the essence of the inward-and-outward contemplation of the body in the body.
sbh3.2:52.12: Again, resolve on the four formless aggregates, by grasping the imagined sign governed by hearing and reflection, in three portions: on the śamatha side, the distraction side, and the vipaśyanā side.
sbh3.2:52.13: When you gather the mind inward, there [are] the four formless aggregates beginning with feeling, having the modes of the perceptions of signlessness, non-conceptuality, and calm, and of non-activity, non-longing, non-agitation, and the pleasure of extinction free of burning, with non-distraction as their object.
sbh3.2:52.14: Resolve [thus]: ‘Moment by moment they proceed, each different from the last, ever new and never old.’
sbh3.2:52.15: This will be for you the essence of the [Conjectural: inward] contemplation in feelings, mind, and dharmas.
sbh3.2:52.16: Those [aggregates] that previously took up sense-objects and had sense-objects as their object, fallen into the unconcentrated stage, gone by, exhausted — and those that arise now, when through forgetfulness there is distraction of mind, the four formless aggregates beginning with feeling, governed by signs, vitarkas, and secondary defilements as their object — resolve on their being subject to coming and going, lasting only a while, briefly present, with danger, [Conjectural: unstable], untrustworthy.
sbh3.2:52.17: This will be for you the essence of the outward contemplation in feelings, mind, and dharmas.
sbh3.2:52.18: Again, having taken up the vipaśyanā sign, abiding in attention that bears signs and [Conjectural: concepts] — those four formless aggregates beginning with feeling that arise inwardly, governed by conceptual, sign-bearing objects — resolve on their moment-by-moment newness, never-oldness, and mutual difference, as before.
sbh3.2:52.19: This will be for you the essence of the [Conjectural: inward-and-outward] contemplation in feelings, mind, and dharmas.
sbh3.2:52.20: Thus, taking the *aśubhā*-practice as governing, you will have entered the four foundations of mindfulness. And in the practice of the foundations of mindfulness you must, from time to time, apply yourself to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
sbh3.2:53.1: With mindfulness thus established in the four foundations of mindfulness — whatever village or town you dwell in dependence on — enter that very village or town for alms with a mind inclined, tending, leaning toward it, letting go of the object, the object-sign.
sbh3.2:53.2: [Avoiding] a fierce elephant, a fierce horse, a fierce ox, a fierce [Conjectural: dog], snakes, pits, stumps, thorns, pools, precipices, streams, excrement and gravel, and avoiding bad conduct and [bad] seat and bed — your self is [Conjectural: protected].
sbh3.2:53.3: Toward those object-signs toward which the faculties should [Conjectural: not] be impelled, let the faculties be [Conjectural: restrained] by non-exertion; and toward those signs toward which the faculties are to be impelled, let mindfulness be established in each — so that the defilements do not become active.
sbh3.2:53.4: Thus, with body well guarded, faculties well restrained, mindfulness well established, with your mind on that, eat alms-food in moderation. And with householders and renunciants [Conjectural: speak in measure], speak reasonably, in season, straightforwardly, calmly.
sbh3.2:53.5: Non-dharmic talk is to be avoided by you in every respect. Even dharmic talk, when you talk, is to be carried on without dispute.
sbh3.2:53.6: Why? Because for a person who dwells given to disputatious talk, the mind settles on abundance of talk. With abundance of talk, agitation; with agitation, no calm. For one whose mind is not calmed, the mind is far from concentration.
sbh3.2:53.7: [Conjectural: Having so conducted yourself], quickly, very quickly, with the object not abandoned, [Conjectural: having sat down], practise yoga in śamatha and vipaśyanā with the sign just as taken up, by [Conjectural: perpetual doing and by thoroughgoing doing]; and by application like the kindling of fire by friction, by continuous and respectful application, be one of perpetual practice.
sbh3.2:53.8: And further, set your mind thus: ‘If the whole lifespan of all the people of Jambūdvīpa were now gathered together into mine alone, then with that measureless lifespan, by application to the [Conjectural: yoga of abandonment] and by continuous and respectful application, I would be one of perpetual practice.’
sbh3.2:53.9: And further, set your mind thus: ‘If only, for as long as I live in Jambūdvīpa, I were not to relax from yoga in attention to śamatha and vipaśyanā!’ — that is, knowing the great fruit and great benefit of this very practice of yoga, how much more does he make this resolve for this brief lifespan, this short life, which even at the furthest is a hundred years and, counted precisely, is but [Conjectural: a moment].
sbh3.2:53.10: Thus, instructed in this way, you, of perpetual practice and thoroughgoing practice, will [Conjectural: attain] the goal for the sake of which you have undertaken abandonment.
sbh3.2:53.11: First you will touch a slight pliancy of body and one-pointedness of mind; then, beyond that, you will reach the extensive excellence, worldly and supramundane.
sbh3.2:54.1: Thus this beginner, at his very first work, engaged in *aśubhā*, being urged by a teacher who knows yoga, is rightly urged; and so practising, he practises rightly.
sbh3.2:54.2: As the one to be trained by *aśubhā* [is instructed] in *aśubhā*, so those to be trained by *maitrī* and the rest, down to *ānāpānasmṛti*, are to be understood as appropriate.
sbh3.2:54.3: Here is the difference, which I shall set forth for the other gateways of entry.
sbh3.2:54.4: There, the beginner engaged in cultivating *maitrī*, having taken up outwardly the sign from the friend-side, [Lacuna] and the neutral-side, seated in a suitable place, with attention of the concentrated stage based on the intention for [their] happiness, should first resolve on one friend, one enemy, one neutral.
sbh3.2:54.5: And toward those three sides, equally, with attention based on the intention for their welfare and happiness, the bringing [of happiness] is to be done: ‘May these beings [Conjectural: who desire happiness] be happy’ — namely with blameless sensual happiness, with blameless happiness accompanied by joy, with blameless happiness free of joy.
sbh3.2:54.6: Then afterwards two friends, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, as before, up to all directions and intermediate directions, are resolved on as filled with the three [sides], friend, enemy, and neutral,
sbh3.2:54.7: uninterrupted, where there is no gap, not even the size of the tip of a staff. As with the friend-side, so it is to be understood with the enemy- and neutral-sides.
sbh3.2:54.8: And he does not abandon the *maitrī*-practice; rather, cultivating *maitrī* itself, he enters the foundations of mindfulness.
sbh3.2:54.9: How, again, does he enter? Resolving, he enters: ‘As I am to others deemed a friend, deemed an enemy, and deemed a neutral — I too desire happiness and am averse to suffering’ — this is for him the essence of the inward contemplation of the body in the body.
sbh3.2:54.10: ‘These beings too are friends, enemies, and neutrals to others; as I am, so they too desire happiness and are averse to suffering’ — this is for him the essence of the outward contemplation of the body in the body.
sbh3.2:54.11: ‘As I am, so are these beings; as happiness is to be sought for myself, so, by their equality and likeness with myself, [I act] for my bringing welfare and happiness to these beings’ — this is for him the essence of the inward-and-outward contemplation of the body in the body.
sbh3.2:54.12: And these four foundations of mindfulness, since they have the mixed aggregates as their object, are a foundation of mindfulness with a mixed object.
sbh3.2:54.13: But if the yogī, taking up only the form-sign — the sign of colour and shape, and the sign of intimation — resolves on the friend-, enemy-, and neutral-sides,
sbh3.2:54.14: then only the body-foundation of mindfulness is established. Relying on resolve-attention, he enters real attention with respect to it.
sbh3.2:54.15: And again, resolving, he enters thus: ‘As many as these beings are, measureless, whom I have resolved on with the intention for their welfare and happiness — more measureless still are the beings who, beginning from my prior limit, have passed away in the status of friend, enemy, or neutral: who, having been friends to me, became enemies; having been enemies, became friends or neutrals. By this consideration, all beings whatsoever are equal and alike.
sbh3.2:54.16: There is here no friendship, enmity, or neutrality that is fixed.’ By this very consideration, too, the equal bringing of welfare and happiness is to be done.
sbh3.2:54.17: As from the prior limit, so also from the later limit, while there is still transmigration in saṁsāra; and those beings whom, from the prior limit, I have [Conjectural: not] shown kindness with a loving mind — though they are past, still I show them kindness now, for the sake of my mind's freedom from turbidity and from ill-will.
sbh3.2:54.18: ‘May those beings who have been be happy; and those who have not been — may they be happy in the time to come’ — thus, for one dwelling in *maitrī* established in real attention, whatever flood of merit, flood of wholesomeness there is, the mass of merit belonging to the dwelling in *maitrī* of resolve does not approach a hundredth part of it, nor a thousandth, nor any reckoning, fraction, counting, or comparison. The rest as before.
sbh3.2:55.1: There, the beginner in dependent origination as this-conditionality takes up the sign imagined through [attention] governed by hearing and reflection — namely, the ignorance, the delusion of other beings, by which they take what is directly impermanent as permanent, what is directly impure as pure, what is painful as pleasant, what is non-self as self.
sbh3.2:55.2: These beings are perverted: through the cause of perversion they crave for feelings in this life and for the production of an individual existence hereafter; and craving, having done actions rooted in birth, thereby in the future, with action and defilement as cause [Damaged] produce sheer suffering —
sbh3.2:55.3: having thus taken up the sign, he resolves inwardly: ‘This whole mass of suffering too has come into being in just this way.’
sbh3.2:55.4: And those individual existences — endless, boundless, beginning from the prior limit, whose beginning is not discerned — they too are thus. All the past, future, and present individual existences of these beings, comprised in the mass of suffering, have come into being in just this way, [Conjectural: and will arise] in the future.
sbh3.2:55.5: And this attention to dependent origination as this-conditionality is entirely real attention; there is no [attention] of resolve. [Conjectural: If, further,] he attends to his own present aggregates as dependently arisen,
sbh3.2:55.6: then inwardly, in the body up to the dharmas, he dwells contemplating dharmas.
sbh3.2:55.7: And when he attends to others' present aggregates as dependently arisen, then [Conjectural: outwardly], in the body up to the dharmas, he dwells contemplating dharmas.
sbh3.2:55.8: When he attends to his own and others' past and future aggregates as dependently arisen, then inwardly and outwardly, in the body up to the dharmas, he dwells contemplating dharmas. The rest as before.
sbh3.2:55.9: There, the beginner engaged in the analysis of elements (*dhātuprabheda*), having taken up outwardly the sign of the hardness of earth — namely, from earth, mountain, grass, forest, gravel, clods, jewels, pearls, beryl, [Restored: conch], rock, coral, and the like — resolves on hardness inwardly.
sbh3.2:55.10: Having taken up outwardly the sign of the water-element — namely, from rivers, springs, ponds, wells, and the like; likewise from a great mass of fire — from what is heated by the sun's rays [Conjectural: in summer], or from [Restored: beings seized by fever], or from [Conjectural: dwellings] heated by a great fire; [Restored: likewise], outwardly, from the wind-mass, from the east, south, west, and north winds, up to the wind-disks;
sbh3.2:55.11: those places [Restored: not filled, not fillable] by [Conjectural: what has form] — with holes, hollow, with room — from these he takes up the sign of the space-element; and inwardly he resolves on the water-element, the fire-element, the wind-element, and the space-element. And by imagination governed by hearing and reflection,
sbh3.2:55.12: he thus takes up the sign of the consciousness-element: when the inner eye-base is unimpaired and form has come into view, but the attention born of these is not present, the eye-consciousness born of them does not arise; in the contrary case it arises. So up to mind, dharmas, and mind-consciousness it is to be understood.
sbh3.2:55.13: Having thus taken up the sign, he resolves: ‘[Restored: There is], in this body made of the four great elements, the seed, the element, the lineage, the nature of all these consciousnesses.’
sbh3.2:55.14: He first resolves on these four great elements [Restored: as gross, as limbs and parts]; then on their finer divisions; and so down to the size of a mote [Restored: in a window-beam]; and so, little by little, down to the atom.
sbh3.2:55.15: He resolves on each single limb and part as made up of a [Conjectural: measureless] heap of atoms — what need to speak of the whole body?
sbh3.2:55.16: This is, for one engaged in the analysis of elements, [Restored: the limit of the analysis of elements] as far as the elements that have form go. As for the space-element, further — [Lacuna] And that, in this practice, in the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, he attends with full knowledge of distraction and non-distraction — this is his clear comprehension and [Conjectural: mindfulness].
sbh3.2:56.1: And again, that the urgency sign and the gladdening sign are well taken up — this is his removal of covetousness and dejection.
sbh3.2:56.2: For him thus dwelling ardent — up to ‘[Conjectural: having removed] covetousness and dejection in the world’ — already at the time of first undertaking right practice,
sbh3.2:56.3: a subtle [Conjectural: one-pointedness of mind, and] pliancy of [Conjectural: body and] mind, proceed, [Restored: hard to discern]: whatever ease of mind, ease of body, and workability of mind and body there is for one cultivating śamatha or vipaśyanā — this is the pliancy of body and mind here.
sbh3.2:56.4: His very subtle one-pointedness of mind and pliancy of mind and body, increasing, bring about a gross, easily discerned one-pointedness of mind and pliancy of body — namely by way of a succession of causes bringing it on.
sbh3.2:56.5: ‘For him, not long from now, a gross pliancy of mind and body and one-pointedness of mind, easily discerned, will arise’ — thus far. As its precursor sign, [Restored: an appearance of heaviness on the crown of the head] arises; and that is not a characteristic of harm.
sbh3.2:56.6: Immediately upon its arising, the mental encumbrance belonging to the side of the defilements that obstruct delight in abandonment is abandoned; and by its antidote, workability of mind and pliancy of mind arise.
sbh3.2:56.7: By its arising, great elements [Restored: with wind predominant], favourable to the arising of bodily pliancy, enter the body; and because they enter, the bodily encumbrance departs —
sbh3.2:56.8: [Restored: that which belongs to the side of the defilements that obstruct delight in abandonment]; and by the bodily pliancy that is its antidote the whole body is filled and [Restored: appears as if brimming over].
sbh3.2:56.9: Then, at its first onset, [Restored: exhilaration of mind], [Restored: gladness of mind], and delight in the object accompanied by joy appear in the mind at that time.
sbh3.2:56.10: Beyond that, the surge of pliancy that came at its first onset gradually becomes more slack.
sbh3.2:56.11: And pliancy proceeds in the body too, following it like a shadow; and that [Restored: exhilaration] of mind also subsides;
sbh3.2:56.12: and the mind, in a calm mode, proceeds on its object, [Restored: propped up by śamatha].
sbh3.2:56.13: Beyond that, this beginner-yogī becomes *samanaskāra* (one possessed of attention), and is reckoned as ‘*samanaskāra*’.
sbh3.2:56.14: Why so? Because a limited attention of the concentrated stage, [Restored: belonging to the form realm], has for the first time been obtained by him. Hence he is called *samanaskāra*.
sbh3.2:56.15: Of this beginner who is *samanaskāra*, these are the signs: a limited mind belonging to the form realm has been obtained by him;
sbh3.2:56.16: limited pliancy of body, pliancy of mind, and one-pointedness of mind; he becomes fit and able
sbh3.2:56.17: [Restored: for the practice of] the defilement-purifying object; and his mind-continuum proceeds [Restored: moistened]; and, enveloped by śamatha, his conduct is purified thereby.
sbh3.2:56.18: If he ranges among lust-arousing objects, he does not generate intense obsession by lust; and [if a slight one arises], with a small and inferior [effort], resting on the antidote, by a mere act of attention, [Restored: he is able to dispel it].
sbh3.2:56.19: As with the lust-arousing, so with the aversion-arousing, the delusion-arousing, the occasion for conceit, and the occasion for vitarka it is to be understood.
sbh3.2:56.20: And when he sits in seclusion and sets his mind [on the object], swiftly, very swiftly the mind becomes pliant, and the body too.
sbh3.2:56.21: Bodily encumbrances do not afflict him excessively; the hindrances are not excessively active; nor do perceptions and attentions accompanied by longing, discontent, and anxiety much arise.
sbh3.2:56.22: Even when he has risen and moves about, some measure of pliancy accompanies him in mind and body. Such are the signs, the clear marks, of the beginner who is *samanaskāra*, to be understood.
sbh3.2:57.3: application, guarding, and accumulation; seclusion; [Restored: and likewise oneness];
sbh3.2:57.4: [Restored: having purified the obstacles] — here, the cultivation of attention.
sbh3.2:58.1: [Here ends] the third yoga-position, comprised within the Śrāvakabhūmi of the Yogācārabhūmi.
